Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: McDonald's is a famous, top-dog brand but it fails most Rule Breaker traits: it is not leading an emerging industry, revenue grows about 4-5% a year, and the share price fell about 19% over the past year rather than showing strong momentum. It is a Rule Maker-style compounder, not a Rule Breaker.
summaries.buffett: McDonald's fits much of Buffett's approach: a simple, durable consumer franchise with a world-famous brand, a 46.1% operating margin in 2025 and 50 straight years of dividend increases. The drawbacks are heavy debt ($39,863M) with negative shareholders' equity and a price of about 19-20 times earnings that offers only a modest margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the simplicity, brand and landlord-like franchise economics that turn about 27% of revenue into free cash flow, and the few ways it can fail outright. He would note that much of its high return on capital comes from leverage and that recent traffic weakness shows limits to pricing power.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms McDonald's is a classic stalwart: a well-known business with a simple story of steady unit growth, value meals and buybacks. With earnings growing mid-to-high single digits and a P/E near 20, the PEG is well above 1, so it fits only at a reasonable rather than bargain price.
summaries.fisher: McDonald's is a strong seller with dominant marketing and a disciplined management team, and the NEXT plan (ArchIQ AI platform, remodels, chicken and drinks push) shows commitment to renewal. But its products change slowly, it does not run real R&D, and sales growth potential is limited compared with Fisher's growth ideal.
summaries.graham: McDonald's meets Graham's size, profitability and dividend-record tests, with 50 consecutive years of dividend increases and EPS up from $4.80 (2015) to $11.95 (2025). It fails the valuation tests: the price is about 21 times three-year average earnings and book value is negative, so it would not pass a defensive investor screen.
summaries.thiel: McDonald's is a near-monopoly brand in its niche with excellent distribution, but it has no proprietary technology that is ten times better and it is not built on a secret others missed. It scores as a durable, established franchise rather than a Zero to One company.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on growth, efficiency and big platform shifts; McDonald's offers efficiency (46% operating margin, rising buybacks) but low growth and only a supporting role in AI adoption. The shares' fall to about 19 times forward earnings may interest valuation-minded investors, but it lacks the secular tailwind he typically seeks.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and catalysts; McDonald's U.S. comparable sales slowed to 0.8% in Q2 2026 and the stock is in a downtrend. The Sept 2026 NEXT plan and value resets are possible catalysts, but the setup does not show the momentum and estimate revisions he favours.
summaries.smith: McDonald's fits Terry Smith's 'good company' test well: high returns on operating capital, strong free cash flow and a brand with resilient demand. Its slow growth and leverage are weaker points, and the recent fall in the share price makes 'don't overpay' easier to satisfy than a year ago.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, McDonald's has a very high return on tangible capital, but its earnings yield (operating income about 6.1% of enterprise value) is only middling. It would rank decently but probably not near the top of a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: McDonald's satisfies Akre's first leg (an extraordinary business with high returns) and arguably the second (capable, shareholder-minded management), but the third leg is weak: it reinvests only part of its free cash flow at high returns and pays most of the rest out as dividends and buybacks.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks low-risk, high-uncertainty bets at deep discounts; McDonald's is low-risk but not deeply discounted, as the price stays near 19-20 times earnings during a temporary traffic slump. It fits the 'few ways to lose' half of Dhandho but not the 'heads I win big' half.
summaries.wood: McDonald's is not a disruptive-innovation company: it does not lead in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomics, though it uses AI in drive-thru ordering and its new ArchIQ platform. It falls outside ARK's investment universe.
summaries.ackman: McDonald's matches Pershing Square's criteria of a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating business with high barriers to entry, the kind of franchise model Ackman has favoured. Its high leverage and limited upside at today's price would be the points to weigh.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' idea partly fits: McDonald's uses scale to fund value menus, marketing and the $8.5B NEXT franchisee support. But much of its scale benefit is kept as high margins and real-estate rent rather than consistently passed to customers, unlike Costco or Amazon.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge new markets with technology; McDonald's is a 70-year-old incumbent in a mature market, so his framework does not really apply.
summaries.nash: McDonald's fails most of Nash's hard screens: revenue grows well under 10% a year, debt far exceeds cash, it is not built on a secular trend, and a Nash-style DCF at 12% gives about $84 a share versus a $242.97 price. It passes on profitability, margin and size, but the overall score is about 65 of 130 points.

momentum.evidence: The share price fell from about $298 in October 2025 to $242.97 on October 16, 2026 (about -19%), while the S&P 500 rose.

g4.evidence: Chris Kempczinski has run McDonald's since 2019 and the stock is widely held by large institutions, but there is no famous strategic backer and recent U.S. execution has been criticised.

g6.evidence: Commentators now describe the stock as cheaper than usual, around 19 times forward earnings, rather than overvalued.

simple.evidence: It sells burgers, fries and drinks and collects rent and royalties from franchisees who run about 95% of its more than 45,000 restaurants.

b2.evidence: It has been profitable every year for decades, raised its dividend for 50 consecutive years, and grew diluted EPS from $4.80 in 2015 to $11.95 in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Capital allocation is disciplined and disclosure is clear, but the 2019 firing of CEO Steve Easterbrook (later fined $400,000 by the SEC for misleading investors) and a combined CEO-chairman role since 2024 weigh on governance.

b6.evidence: It avoids large acquisitions and sticks to its core brand, even closing the CosMc's spin-off concept.

roic.evidence: After-tax operating income of about $9.7B in 2025 on roughly $38B of net debt plus equity is a return near 26%, but that capital base depends on $39,863M of debt and negative equity.

fcf.evidence: In 2025 operating cash flow of $10,551M less capex of $3,365M left $7,186M of free cash flow, 84% of $8,563M net income.

b10.evidence: It pays out most profit (2025 dividends $5,115M plus buybacks $2,056M), and the shares, at $242.97, are roughly where they were in October 2021 despite EPS rising from $10.04 (2021) to $11.95 (2025).

safety.evidence: At about 19.7 times trailing EPS of $12.31 and a 4.5% free-cash-flow yield, the price is fair but not well below a conservative value estimate.

fairprice.evidence: About 18.9 times 2026 consensus EPS of $12.89 is reasonable for its quality, but consensus EPS growth of 5.7% for 2026 is modest.

mu5.evidence: The main failure routes are a lasting traffic decline or a debt crunch, and its rent-backed franchise income and $10.6B of yearly operating cash flow make both unlikely.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest about $3B a year in new restaurants and remodels at good returns, but that is well under its free cash flow, so most profit is returned rather than reinvested.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic stalwart: steady 4-5% revenue growth, high margins, buybacks and a rising dividend.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 19.7 is far above its expected earnings growth of roughly 6-7% a year.

runway.evidence: It expects new restaurants to add about 2.5% to systemwide sales growth in 2027 and about 2% by 2030, plus share gains in chicken and drinks, but no large new categories.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 751.8M in 2021 to 711.1M in Q2 2026 through buybacks, but there is no notable open-market insider buying.

ly8.evidence: It is one of the most widely followed stocks, with about 34 analysts covering it.

fi2.evidence: It keeps adding items such as the Big Arch, new beverages and hand-breaded chicken, though the core menu changes slowly.

fi3.evidence: McDonald's does not report R&D spending, and results of its menu and technology tests are not separately disclosed.

fi4.evidence: It runs the largest marketing machine in fast food and has nearly 220 million active loyalty members across 70 markets.

longterm.evidence: Its McDonald's > NEXT plan commits about $8.5B of franchisee support through 2036 for remodels, AI tools and value, accepting near-term costs.

gr1.evidence: It had $26,885M of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $172B.

ni10.evidence: Net income was positive every year from 2016 ($4,686.5M) to 2025 ($8,563M).

gr4.evidence: It has paid dividends since 1976 and in September 2026 announced its 50th consecutive annual increase, to $1.93 a quarter.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $4.80 in 2015 to $11.95 in 2025, an increase of about 149%.

gr6.evidence: The price of $242.97 is about 21 times average diluted EPS of $11.63 over 2023-2025.

gr7.evidence: Shareholders' equity was -$1,023M at June 30, 2026, so price/book is negative and the test cannot be met.

th1.evidence: Its advantage is brand, scale and real estate, not proprietary technology ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: AI ordering and digital loyalty help now, but lower-income consumer pressure and high beef costs make 2026 a difficult moment.

th3.evidence: It already holds a large share of a huge, mature market rather than dominating a small one.

team.evidence: Management is experienced and disciplined, but it is not a founder-led or exceptional team, and U.S. sales execution faltered in 2025-26.

th5.evidence: Its 45,000+ restaurants, drive-thrus, app and delivery partners give it unmatched reach to customers.

durable.evidence: McDonald's has led global fast food for decades and its brand, sites and franchise system are very hard to disrupt within 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Its strategy of value, chicken, drinks and digital is the same one rivals pursue.

trend.evidence: It uses AI (Archy drive-thru voice AI at over 90% accuracy) but is not a leading beneficiary of a platform shift.

dr1.evidence: 2026 consensus EPS growth is about 5.7% and U.S. comparable sales slowed to 0.8% in Q2 2026, so earnings are not accelerating.

dr2.evidence: If the NEXT remodels, value resets and Make It Golden programme lift traffic, results could improve by 2028, but the benefit is uncertain and partly expected.

dr4.evidence: Lower rates would ease its interest bill ($1,582M in 2025), but a squeezed lower-income consumer and high beef prices work against it.

dr6.evidence: Possible catalysts are the NEXT rollout, the October 2026 Make It Golden launch and new chicken and drink lines.

dr7.evidence: Slowing traffic and a falling share price do not support high-conviction concentration for a momentum-led investor.

gm.evidence: McDonald's does not report gross margin; its operating margin of 46.1% in 2025 reflects franchise rent and royalties rather than product pricing.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $7,761M against a market value of about $172B is a yield of about 4.5%, reasonable for its quality.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of $12,805M is about 6.1% of an enterprise value of about $211B, a middling earnings yield.

pa2.evidence: The 2025-26 U.S. traffic slump looks tied to fixable value pricing and execution, which management is addressing with new value menus and leadership changes.

pa4.evidence: A world-famous brand with $10.6B of yearly operating cash flow makes a permanent loss of capital unlikely, though valuation can shrink.

wo1.evidence: It is a restaurant company, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics.

wo2.evidence: Its costs (beef, labor) are rising, not falling rapidly with volume.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its market grows in low single digits and will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Franchise rent and royalties cushion it, but beef costs, wages and interest rates still affect its company-run restaurants and franchisees.

ns1.evidence: It funds value menus and $8.5B of NEXT support, but it keeps much of its scale advantage as high margins rather than passing it on.

ns4.evidence: If NEXT works, it should be stronger in chicken, drinks and digital by 2036, but that is not clearly assured.

va2.evidence: It solves the everyday need for a quick, cheap meal, a large but not painful problem.

tn1.evidence: It is a 70-year-old restaurant business adding AI tools, not a company built for a secular trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees a burger chain, while much of its income is rent from a property portfolio, a gap that is already widely known.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap U.S. company and not in any of the zones Nash avoids.

tn4.evidence: It passes on revenue growth (up in four of five years to $26,885M in 2025) and profitability ($8,563M net income) but fails cash versus debt ($822M vs $39,863M), with no infrastructure-style excuse.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive each quarter (Q2 2026: $1,976M), but debt has exceeded cash in every quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 3.7% in 2025 and 3.7% in Q2 2026.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 3.7% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 26.7% gives about 30, below 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 3.7% while total operating costs grew 2.0% ($14,208M to $14,492M).

tn9.evidence: It hits instant kills: debt of $39,863M far exceeds cash of $822M, and revenue growth is below 10%.

tn10.evidence: There is no existential threat, but it faces joint-employer and wage regulation, franchisee lawsuits and food-safety litigation such as the 2024 E. coli outbreak.

tn11.evidence: McDonald's provides fast, affordable, familiar meals that help busy people eat cheaply and quickly, and charges franchisees rent and royalties plus sales at its own restaurants.

tn13.evidence: Total about 65: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 0, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture 5, talent 0. (short interest and institutional ownership scored from its usual large-cap profile, not checked this month)

tn14.evidence: Revenue dipped in 2022, operating margin fell to 40.4% that year, free cash flow fell in 2022 and 2024, and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is 7.8x and the current ratio 1.08, but non-goodwill assets of $56,573M are below total liabilities of $60,943M and equity is negative.

tn18.evidence: Kempczinski grew operating income from $7,324M (2020) to $12,393M (2025), but he has been CEO since 2019 (under 10 years), is not a founder and has no notable open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: It beat EPS estimates in Q1 2026 ($2.83 vs $2.74) and Q2 2026, but U.S. comparable sales have fallen short of expectations in recent quarters.

tn21.evidence: No fraud, auditor change or acquisition spree, but the CEO is also chairman and the 2019 Easterbrook affair was a governance lapse.

tn22.evidence: It has strong revenue and profits and shrinks its share count through buybacks.

tn24.evidence: A 4.5% free-cash-flow yield implies roughly 5% a year of growth at a 10% required return, about what it delivers (revenue CAGR 5.1% over 2022-2025).

tn25.evidence: Using 5.1% growth, a 27.0% free-cash-flow margin, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate less $39,041M of net debt gives about $84 a share, well below $242.97.

tn26.evidence: About 18.9 times 2026 EPS is in line with restaurant peers, but with 5.7% EPS growth the PEG is about 3.3.
